answers.text: Since 1970 the 10y-3m inversion has a strong record: every recession was preceded by one, and inversions were followed by recessions through the period this source covers. That supports it as a strong signal.
A 12-month window is not dependable. Lead times are cited as 7 to 24 months, so a recession can start well after 12 months, and an on-time recession is not guaranteed.
The most recent inversion looks like a false signal so far. A widely predicted recession did not materialize and growth stayed steady, and many bond strategists lost confidence in the indicator.

The clean record rests on only about eight episodes, and critics dispute how reliable it is. A short inversion, such as the 8-day one in 2019, shows that signal definitions matter. Treat it as a strong warning, not a reliable 12-month predictor.

answers.text: No evidence here shows gold is always a safe haven. The sources only say gold has a safe-haven role in uncertain periods, and one of them is an industry body that promotes gold. Neither gives crash-by-crash returns.
These sources contain no price data for 2008, March 2020 or other equity crashes. Whether gold rose or fell in those episodes cannot be judged from them.
Gold's price is driven mainly by sentiment, so its behavior depends on investor mood rather than a fixed rule. That makes a guaranteed crash hedge unlikely.
Gold's safe-haven appeal is shown more clearly in geopolitical stress, such as the June 2025 surge. Investors can also rotate away from gold, as the early-2025 move into platinum shows.
Gold carries no credit risk and is liquid, which supports a hedging role. But one cited long-run figure (a dollar in gold from 1801 to 1998 worth 78 cents) shows it does not reliably preserve value.

answers.text: Not reliably. Evidence is mixed: some studies show gains (a 13% call-center increase, small productivity gains in US data), while others show declines in an IT setting or lower manager-perceived productivity.

Hybrid has the clearer positive evidence here, though it is self-reported: employees say hybrid improves their productivity, and fewer office interruptions are a cited mechanism for gains in remote or hybrid work.

For fully remote work, the evidence is mixed. Gains are reported for specific tasks like call-center work, but more remote time was linked to lower manager-perceived productivity and culture is harder to build.
Time saved by working from home may add to productivity: workers put 40% of commute time savings into their jobs. This is an indirect channel and does not measure output.

The amount of remote time may matter. Working remotely more than 2.5 days per week was tied to weaker coworker relationships, which suggests limits for heavily remote setups. These sources give no direct fully-remote vs hybrid productivity comparison.

answers.text: Yes, three URLs per call fits within the five-URL limit, and results come back one per URL in the order sent. You must avoid duplicate URLs, which cause a 400.
Individual failures are recoverable: a failed URL returns status "failed" with an error inside a 200 response and is not charged, so keep the successes and retry or drop the failures.
Check each result, not only the call: a result marked succeeded can still be an error page, and not every provider reports http_status, so also inspect warnings.
Avoid pinning providers if you want per-URL recovery: if pinned providers fail on every URL, the whole call returns a 502 instead of per-URL failures.

answers.text: These sources do not show that gold is always a safe haven. They give no price data for 2008, March 2020 or other equity crashes, so those episodes cannot be verified from them.

The case for gold as a haven is mainly an industry claim: the World Gold Council cites its safe-haven status in uncertain periods and its lack of credit risk. That is advocacy, not crash-by-crash evidence.
Gold's price depends mainly on sentiment, and investors sometimes rotate out of it. So a flight to safety is not guaranteed in every crash.
The only concrete haven example is a June 2025 geopolitical spike, a geopolitical episode rather than an equity crash. It does not settle how gold behaves in market crashes like 2008 or 2020.

Gold's long-run record is not uniformly protective: one cited example shows a dollar in gold from 1801 to 1998 ending below its starting value. This is a long-horizon caveat, not a crash-specific result.

answers.text: Probably associated with lower risk, but only as observational evidence: a meta-analysis of 28 prospective studies links each daily cup to 6–9% lower type 2 diabetes risk. These sources show no randomized trial proving causation.
The evidence is observational and cohort-based. Reviews say coffee 'may reduce' risk, which is hedged wording that does not establish cause. Confounding and study heterogeneity remain open caveats.

'Moderate' is not defined specifically for diabetes in these sources. Related reviews treat about 3–4 cups/day as usual or beneficial and up to 5 cups (~400 mg caffeine) as safe, but those figures are general and mostly cardiovascular.

The association is dose-dependent per cup and appears for both caffeinated (9%) and decaffeinated (6%) coffee. This suggests caffeine is not the only possible factor, though the sources do not identify a mechanism.

answers.text: Sometimes, but not reliably. Findings are mixed: some studies show gains (e.g., a 13% rise in a call-center study, small economy-wide gains), while others show declines, notably in an IT setting.

Hybrid work: the evidence here is mostly self-reported. Employees say hybrid arrangements improve their productivity, and quieter home time suits focused work. Hard output data for hybrid is thin in these sources.

Fully or highly remote work looks riskier: more time remote was linked to lower manager-perceived productivity, and culture is harder to build when fully remote. These sources lack a clean fully remote vs hybrid output comparison.
A plausible mechanism for gains is time and focus: fewer office interruptions help concentration-heavy work, and commute savings partly go to work (40% of saved time).
